2. A server in a cluster is called a "node." I will not write "replica" or "instance."

# Distributed Systems at Depth: A Reference for Senior Backend Engineers

## Introduction

Ask ten backend engineers what makes distributed systems hard and you will get ten answers involving networks, clocks, or failure. All of them are partly right, but none captures the core difficulty. A distributed system is a set of independent processes that must agree on shared state while communicating over a medium that can delay, reorder, duplicate, or silently drop messages. When one machine's memory is replaced by several nodes joined by a network, the assumptions that make ordinary programming tractable stop holding. A function call either returns or fails. A remote call may do neither: it may succeed on the far side, fail visibly, or leave the caller with no way to know which happened.

This guide is for engineers who already build and operate backend services and need a precise model of what those services do when they span machines. It is not an introduction to networking, and it is not a survey of every consensus protocol in the literature. Its aim is to give you the vocabulary, the failure models, and the trade-off reasoning that let you design, review, and debug systems whose correctness depends on timing, partial failure, and concurrency.

Throughout the guide we will use one running example: **Kestrel**, a payments ledger. Kestrel records debits and credits against customer accounts, and its invariants are unforgiving. Money must not be created or destroyed. A transfer must not be applied twice. A balance read after a successful write must reflect that write for the customer who made it. Kestrel runs on 5 nodes across 3 regions, placed 2-2-1: two regions host two nodes each, and the third hosts one.

That layout is deliberate, and it shows the kind of reasoning this guide asks you to practice. With 5 nodes, a majority is 3, so the cluster commits writes as long as any 2 nodes are unavailable. Losing any single region still leaves at least 3 nodes reachable, so writes continue. Losing one of the two-node regions leaves exactly 3, which is the minimum for a majority. Losing the single-node region leaves 4. Each of these claims follows from arithmetic, but the arithmetic is only useful if you know which failures it is meant to survive, and whether the survival covers the failures you actually expect. Later sections return to Kestrel's layout and test it against specific failure scenarios.

The guide is organized in roughly this order:

- **Time, clocks, and ordering.** Why wall-clock timestamps cannot order events across nodes, and what does instead.
- **Failure models and detection.** Crash, omission, and Byzantine faults; how timeouts and heartbeats turn uncertainty into suspicion; why a failure detector can be wrong.
- **Quorums and consensus.** How majority quorums give safety, how leader election and log replication build on them, and what they cost in latency.
- **Transactions across nodes.** Atomic commit, its blocking failure modes, and how Kestrel keeps transfers correct without a global lock.
- **Idempotency and delivery semantics.** Why "exactly once" is a property you build rather than receive, and how to make retries safe.
- **Operating and observing the system.** The metrics, traces, and runbooks that tell you whether a cluster is healthy, and how to diagnose it when it is not.

Each section aims for roughly 1,000 to 1,400 words. Code examples are in Go and are written to be read as reference material. They illustrate the mechanism, and they are not production-ready libraries. Where a section includes a worked example, it uses Kestrel, so the same ledger's behavior accumulates into a single consistent picture across the guide.

Read the sections in order if you are new to the material. If you already run distributed systems, treat each section as a checklist against your own designs, and check whether your system's assumptions about time, failure, and ordering match what the section describes.

Key takeaway: In a distributed system, a remote operation can fail in ways a local call cannot, including leaving the outcome unknown, so correctness has to be designed around partial failure from the start.

# Six Core Ideas Behind Consensus

Consensus protocols look different on the surface. Raft is organized around a leader and a replicated log, Paxos around proposal numbers and two-phase voting, and Zab around epochs and a totally ordered history. Underneath, they rely on the same few ideas. These six are the ones that determine whether a consensus implementation is correct, and most subtle consensus bugs trace back to one of them.

Throughout, the running example is **Kestrel**, our payments ledger on 5 nodes across 3 regions: N1 and N2 in region A, N3 and N4 in region B, and N5 in region C. A write commits when 3 nodes hold it.

## 1. Quorum Intersection Is the Source of Safety

Every protocol here commits a decision only after a majority of nodes acknowledges it. The reason is not that majorities are fast. Any two majorities of the same set must share at least one node. If Kestrel commits transfer T1 on {N1, N2, N3} and a later leader gathers votes from {N3, N4, N5}, the overlap at N3 carries knowledge of T1 into the new leader's view. Safety rests on this overlap.

The intersection property is what makes the quorum size matter. For n nodes, the quorum is ⌊n/2⌋+1. Kestrel's quorum is 3 of 5, so it tolerates 2 node failures. Two intersecting quorums also mean that *two different values cannot both commit*, because the second decision's quorum would have to include some node that already voted for the first.

Senior engineers should watch for two mistakes. The first is even-sized clusters. Four nodes still need a quorum of 3, so they tolerate only 1 failure, the same as three nodes, and they add a point of cost without adding resilience. The second is "flexible quorums," where the read and write quorums differ in size. Those are safe only when every read quorum intersects every write quorum that could have committed recent state. Changing quorum sizes without checking this overlap is how split-brain bugs get introduced.

## 2. Terms, Epochs, and Ballots Fence Out Stale Leaders

A leader that has been partitioned away does not know it has been replaced. Consensus protocols handle this with a monotonically increasing number attached to every leadership attempt: a **term** in Raft, a **ballot** or proposal number in Paxos, and an **epoch** in Zab. Any message carrying a lower number is rejected.

Suppose Kestrel's leader N1 is in term 7 and gets cut off from regions B and C. Region A's N2 cannot form a majority alone, so no new leader emerges there. Meanwhile N3 wins term 8 with votes from N3, N4, and N5. If N1 reconnects and tries to commit a debit in term 7, N3 rejects it, because term 7 is older than the term N3 has already seen. N1 steps down on seeing the higher term.

This is a fencing mechanism, and it matters beyond the consensus layer. A deposed leader can still believe it holds authority while a downstream payment rail is talking to it. Kestrel passes its current term as a fencing token to the rail, and the rail rejects any command whose token is below the highest token it has seen. Without this step, a leader that is correct about its own log can still cause a double payout.

Terms must be persisted before a node acts on them. A node that forgets its current term after a crash can vote twice in the same term, and two leaders can then be elected under the same number.

## 3. The Election Restriction Keeps Committed Entries Alive

A new leader must hold every committed entry. Raft ensures this at election time instead of repairing the log afterward. A voter grants its vote only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date as its own, where "up to date" means the candidate's last entry has a higher term, or the same term and a greater or equal index.

Here is the check in Go, following the structure of the Raft rules:

```go
// upToDate reports whether a candidate's log is at least as current as ours.
// Logs are compared by the term of the last entry first, then by length.
func upToDate(candTerm, candIndex, myTerm, myIndex uint64) bool {
	if candTerm != myTerm {
		return candTerm > myTerm
	}
	return candIndex >= myIndex
}

func (n *Node) handleRequestVote(req VoteRequest) VoteResponse {
	if req.Term < n.currentTerm {
		return VoteResponse{Term: n.currentTerm, Granted: false}
	}
	if req.Term > n.currentTerm {
		n.becomeFollower(req.Term) // persists the new term before responding
	}

	lastTerm, lastIndex := n.lastLogTermIndex()
	canVote := n.votedFor == 0 || n.votedFor == req.CandidateID
	if canVote && upToDate(req.LastLogTerm, req.LastLogIndex, lastTerm, lastIndex) {
		n.votedFor = req.CandidateID // must be persisted before the reply is sent
		return VoteResponse{Term: n.currentTerm, Granted: true}
	}
	return VoteResponse{Term: n.currentTerm, Granted: false}
}
```

The reasoning is the intersection argument from section 1. A committed entry sits on a majority, and any winning candidate collects votes from a majority, so at least one voter holds the committed entry. That voter refuses any candidate whose log lacks it. The winner therefore already has every committed entry.

Zab takes a different route to the same guarantee. In its discovery phase, the new leader collects the histories of a quorum and selects the one with the highest accepted epoch, breaking ties by the highest zxid, which is a (epoch, counter) pair. The effect is equivalent: the chosen history contains everything that could have been committed. The difference is where the work happens. Raft filters at vote time, while Zab selects during recovery.

## 4. Commit Rules Are Subtler Than "Majority Has It"

Possessing an entry on a majority does not, by itself, make it safe to report as committed. Raft's commit rule is precise: a leader commits an entry from its *own* term once it is stored on a majority. Earlier-term entries become committed only indirectly, when a later entry from the current term commits after them.

The reason is a scenario from the Raft paper, often called the Figure 8 problem. Kestrel's leader N1 in term 2 writes entry X at index 3 and copies it to N2. Before committing, N1 crashes. N5 wins term 3 with votes from N3, N4, and N5, none of which hold X, and writes its own entry Y at index 3. Suppose N5 then crashes and N1 returns, wins term 4, and copies its entry at index 3 to a majority. If N1 treats that as commitment and reports X to the customer, and then N5 wins a later term without X, the ledger reports a transfer as committed that the cluster later discards. The rule prevents this: N1 does not commit the old entry directly. It commits a term-4 entry, and everything before it commits along with that entry.

Zab achieves the same effect through its ordering discipline: proposals are delivered in zxid order, and a proposal is committed only after all earlier proposals in its epoch are delivered. Any implementation that reports a write as durable must enforce the commit rule exactly. Relaxing it to "a majority has the bytes" is a common and dangerous shortcut.

## 5. Paxos Recovers Accepted Values Through Two Phases

Paxos is often taught as a single algorithm, but its core is a rule about recovery. Phase 1 (Prepare) has a proposer send a proposal number *n* to a majority. Each acceptor promises not to accept anything numbered below *n*, and it reports the highest-numbered value it has already accepted. Phase 2 (Accept) has the proposer send a value to the acceptors.

The key rule is in the second phase. If any acceptor in the promise responses reports a previously accepted value, the proposer *must* propose the value with the highest proposal number among those reports. It may propose its own value only if no acceptor has accepted anything. This is what prevents an in-flight decision from being overwritten.

Consider Kestrel deciding the outcome of transfer T1. Proposer P1 gets promises from N1, N2, and N3. N2 reports that it accepted "T1 = debit A, credit B" under number 5 before a failure. P1 must propose that value, even if P1 originally wanted to propose something different. A proposer that ignores the reports can produce two different decisions for the same slot, and nothing in the protocol will stop it.

Multi-Paxos amortizes the cost by electing a stable leader who skips Phase 1 for subsequent slots. This is a performance optimization, and it is also where most production Paxos implementations diverge from the paper. The leader-election step becomes a separate component whose correctness is required for safety, and the protocol's proofs do not cover it. Engineers who implement Multi-Paxos should treat the leader lease and the prepare step as safety-critical code.

## 6. Linearizable Reads Are Not Free

A consensus protocol that orders writes does not automatically give correct reads. A node that believes it is leader may have been deposed without knowing it. If it answers a read from its local state, the client may see a balance that predates a write already acknowledged elsewhere. That violates linearizability, which requires that a read reflect every write that completed before the read began.

There are three standard approaches, with different trade-offs:

- **Log the read.** Treat the read as a log entry and commit it. This is always correct and always expensive, since every read takes a full quorum round trip.
- **ReadIndex.** The leader records its current commit index, confirms it is still leader by collecting heartbeat acknowledgments from a majority, waits until its state machine has applied up to that index, and then serves the read locally. This costs one quorum round trip without writing to the log.
- **Leader leases.** The leader serves reads locally while holding a lease granted by a majority, valid for a bounded interval. This is the fastest option, but it depends on clock assumptions. If the clock drift bound is violated, the lease can outlive the leader's real authority, and reads can be stale.

For Kestrel, balance queries use ReadIndex. The 2-2-1 layout makes the cost visible: a read that needs acknowledgments from N3 in region B and N5 in region C pays cross-region latency on every call. Teams often choose leases to hide that latency, then discover during a clock incident that the bounded-drift assumption was never checked. If you use leases, measure the clock error bound in production and alarm when it approaches the lease length.

Key takeaway: Consensus safety comes from quorum intersection, fenced by monotonically increasing terms, with commit rules and leader selection built to preserve every decision a majority may have accepted, while correct reads require an explicit check that the leader's authority is still current.

# Trade-offs in Consensus Algorithms, Illustrated by Failures

Consensus protocols do not offer free safety, speed, and availability. Each design choice moves cost somewhere else, and the cost usually shows up during an incident rather than in a benchmark. The stories below use **Kestrel**, our payments ledger on 5 nodes across 3 regions (N1 and N2 in region A, N3 and N4 in region B, N5 in region C), with a write quorum of 3. They are composites of failure patterns that appear repeatedly in production systems, not records of one event.

## 1. Election Timeout: Availability Versus Disruption

Raft and Zab both detect a dead leader by timing out. A short timeout recovers quickly from a real failure but misreads a slow leader as dead. A long timeout avoids false alarms but leaves the cluster unable to commit for longer after a real crash.

The randomized timeout is the standard mitigation, and its floor is the important number:

```go
// electionTimeout returns a randomized timeout so that followers do not
// start elections in lockstep. The base must exceed the cross-region
// round-trip p99 plus heartbeat jitter, or healthy leaders get deposed.
func electionTimeout(base, jitter time.Duration) time.Duration {
	return base + time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(jitter)))
}
```

**The failure story.** Kestrel's team set the base timeout to 300 ms, which was fine in the single-region test environment. After the cluster spread across regions, a routine network degradation between region A and region B pushed p99 round-trip time to about 400 ms. Heartbeats from the leader arrived late, followers started elections, and each election briefly stopped writes. The new leader then received heartbeats from the old one, which had not actually failed. Within an hour the cluster held roughly 40 elections, and payment throughput fell to a fraction of normal because every election forced in-flight commits to be re-driven.

The fix had two parts. The base timeout moved to 1.5 seconds with 1.5 seconds of jitter, and the team enabled **pre-vote**, a Raft extension in which a node first asks whether an election would succeed before incrementing its term. Pre-vote matters for a different case: a node cut off from the cluster keeps timing out and inflating its term. When it reconnects, its high term forces the healthy leader to step down, even though the cluster was fine. Pre-vote stops the partitioned node from forcing that disruption.

The trade-off is explicit: a 1.5-second base means a real leader crash costs roughly 1.5 to 3 seconds of unavailability for writes. Kestrel accepts this because its customers prefer a short pause to duplicated or disrupted payment processing. A ledger tuned for a lower-latency product might make the opposite choice.

## 2. Durability Versus Latency: The fsync Decision

Consensus safety depends on nodes not forgetting promises. In Raft, a node must persist its current term and its vote before replying to a vote request. In Paxos, an acceptor must persist its promise and accepted value before responding. Zab requires the same for its epoch and proposal log. Each of these requires an fsync, and fsync is the most expensive operation on the write path.

**The failure story.** To cut write latency, an engineer on Kestrel's storage team disabled fsync on the log for nodes in region B, reasoning that the other nodes provided durability. For three weeks this worked. Then a power event in region B's data center restarted N3 and N4 with the last few hundred milliseconds of their logs lost. N3 had voted for N4 in term 12 before the crash; after restart it had no record of the vote and no record of term 12. It voted again in term 12 for a different candidate, and the cluster briefly had two leaders in the same term.

The cluster detected the problem only because a term-12 write from one leader was rejected by a majority that had recorded the other. The protocol's guarantee of at most one leader per term was broken, and the consequence was a window where two leaders each believed they could commit. Kestrel's fencing tokens from the earlier design caught the stale writes, but the team spent two days reconciling the ledger against the payment rail's records to confirm no transfer had settled twice.

The correct trade-off is not "always fsync" versus "never fsync." Batching, group commit, and battery-backed write caches all reduce cost while preserving the ordering that fsync provides. Kestrel now batches promise and vote writes into a single fsync per election step, and it refuses to start if the storage layer reports that write barriers are disabled. The rule for practitioners is that durability settings are part of the consensus safety argument, and a change to them needs the same review as a change to the protocol.

## 3. Read Latency Versus Correctness: Leases and Clocks

Section 6 of the previous discussion described three read strategies. The trade-off among them is latency against dependence on assumptions. Log reads are always correct and always slow. ReadIndex costs a quorum round trip. Leader leases are fast, since the leader answers from local state, but they are only correct if no node's clock drifts past the bound the lease was computed with.

**The failure story.** Kestrel's balance API served reads from the leader under a 2-second lease. A VM hosting N1 in region A experienced a multi-second pause when its hypervisor was overcommitted, a condition the guest could not observe. When the pause ended, N1's lease check used its local clock, which had not advanced during the pause in its perception but had advanced in real time. N1 believed its lease was valid, though N3 had already been elected in a higher term and had committed a transfer. N1 served a balance that omitted the transfer, and a customer saw a balance that was wrong for about four seconds, long enough to trigger a duplicate payment attempt.

The lesson is that a lease is a claim about time, and time in virtual machines is not monotonic from the application's point of view. The team made three changes. They switched lease checks to a monotonic clock source for intervals, not wall-clock time. They subtracted a measured clock-error bound from every lease, sized from production telemetry. And they added a self-check: after any scheduling gap longer than a threshold, the leader revalidates its lease through a ReadIndex round before serving reads.

The trade-off remains. Leases still save a quorum round trip on most reads, which matters for Kestrel's cross-region layout. Teams that adopt them should measure clock error continuously rather than assuming a constant.

## 4. Membership Changes: Safety During Reconfiguration

Nodes are added and removed over a cluster's lifetime. Naively switching from one membership configuration to another is unsafe, because during the transition the old and new configurations can each form a majority that does not intersect the other. Raft solves this with joint consensus, in which the cluster temporarily requires majorities of both the old and new configurations. Single-node changes, one at a time, are another safe approach that Raft's authors describe and that many implementations use.

**The failure story.** Kestrel's operators replaced N4 with N6 by issuing two configuration commands in quick succession from a script that did not wait for the first to commit. The first command removed N4 from the configuration while a partition separated region B from the rest. The second added N6 in a different region. For a brief interval, the cluster had configurations that allowed two disjoint majorities, and two leaders were elected for different slots of the ledger. The divergence was caught during reconciliation, but it left a set of entries that had to be manually resolved.

The fix was procedural and protocol-level. The tooling now refuses to issue a second membership change until the first is committed, and the cluster enforces single-node changes at the protocol layer. The team also adopted a rule that a 5-node cluster should never be reconfigured to 6 nodes: at 6 nodes the quorum rises to 4, which tolerates only 2 failures, the same as 5 nodes, while adding cross-region cost. The right answer for Kestrel's growth was to move to a 7-node layout, which tolerates 3 failures, and to change the membership one step at a time.

## 5. Flexibility Versus Liveness: Paxos Dueling Proposers

Basic Paxos is flexible. Any node can propose, and there is no designated leader to fail. This flexibility is also a liveness hazard. Two proposers can keep preempting each other: each Prepare with a higher number invalidates the other's Accept, and both retry with still higher numbers, indefinitely. Safety holds throughout, because the protocol never decides two values, but no value is decided either.

**The failure story.** Kestrel's batch settlement job, a Paxos-driven ledger process, ran from two regions at the same time after a scheduler change. Both proposers started at the same moment, sent Prepare messages, and each time one proposer's Accept arrived, the other had already raised its number. Commit throughput dropped to near zero, and the logs showed proposal numbers climbing by thousands per minute. Nothing was incorrect, but no settlements completed for the duration.

The remedy is a designated proposer, which is Multi-Paxos with a stable leader, or randomized backoff before retrying. The trade-off is that a designated leader reintroduces leader election, and election is where the subtle bugs live. Teams should treat the choice of proposer as a liveness decision and decide explicitly how the system behaves when two proposers exist, not discover it during a settlement backlog.

## 6. Recovery Time Versus Log Size: Zab Synchronization

Zab, the protocol behind ZooKeeper, separates leader election from history synchronization. After a new leader is chosen, it must bring a quorum of followers up to its history before it can accept new proposals. The cost of that synchronization grows with the amount of history a follower lacks. Snapshots shorten it, but snapshots themselves cost I/O, and frequent snapshots have their own latency impact.

**The failure story.** A coordination service backing Kestrel's configuration store had been running for months without snapshot tuning, and its transaction log had grown large. When the leader failed, the newly elected leader had to send a long tail of transactions to two followers that had been offline for maintenance. Synchronization took more than 40 seconds, during which the configuration store refused writes. Kestrel's routing layer, which reads configuration on every transfer, backed off and then failed transfers that exceeded its own deadline. The incident was a coordination-layer outage caused by log growth, and it looked like a leader failure from the outside.

The fix combined more frequent snapshots, a bounded retention policy for the transaction log, and a monitoring alert on follower lag measured in transactions rather than in time. The trade-off is clear: aggressive snapshotting increases steady-state I/O and CPU, and Kestrel accepted that cost to keep recovery bounded. Teams should measure the worst-case recovery time they can tolerate and size snapshot cadence from that number.

Snapshot transfer has a related hazard in Raft. A node far behind receives a large snapshot that saturates the leader's network link. Heartbeats stall behind the bulk transfer, followers time out, and the cluster elects a new leader it did not need. The mitigation is to rate-limit snapshot transfer and to give heartbeats their own priority on the connection.

## Summary of the Trade-offs

Each trade-off above has the same shape. A knob that looks like a performance setting changes a safety or liveness property, and the failure appears only when the system is stressed in a way the test environment did not reproduce. The election timeout, the fsync setting, the lease bound, the membership procedure, the proposer count, and the snapshot cadence each deserve a documented rationale and a review whenever they change. The consensus protocol gives you guarantees only for the configuration you actually run.

Key takeaway: Every consensus trade-off moves cost between latency, availability, and assumptions about time and disk, and the failures they produce look like outages in other components unless the team measures the specific property each knob governs.
